newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia govt has not changed grain harvest forecast.
newsitem.headline: Russia govt has not changed grain harvest forecast.

text.p: The Russian government has not revised its 1996 net grain harvest forecast of 75-77 million tonnes, even though a senior agriculture official sees output at less than 74 million, government sources said on Wednesday.
Ivan Kaglashkin, an agriculture specialist at the government's farm section, said the government had not lowered its official forecast at a closed meeting on Tuesday.
But he and other officials said there were top-level concerns over how the Siberian harvest was progressing.
"At yesterday's Food Commission meeting, the figure 75 (million tonnes net harvest) was heard," Kaglashkin said.
"The 75-77 million tonne figure is still valid, but it depends on how the weather affects the pace of the harvest.
"We are not yet considering a lower figure."
Interfax news agency quoted First Deputy Agriculture Minister Vladimir Shcherbak as telling the meeting Russia's 1996 net grain harvest would exceed last year's by 10 million tonnes.
Last year's output was officially 63.4 million tonnes.
An aide to Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Zaveryukha, whose portfolio includes the harvest, said Zaveryukha was disturbed by Siberia's wet weather, which threatened grain quality.
"Without question it worries him," said the aide.
"For a month and a half there has been variable but rainy weather in Siberia just as the harvest gets under way."
Some farm specialists worry that parts of cereals crops may be ruined or left to rot as a result of delayed harvesting.

A source at the State Meteorological Service said crops specialists there saw no grounds for the government to change its forecast, but said five percent of cereals crops in the Urals and Siberia could go unharvested due to cold rains.
Kaglashkin said Moscow expected farmers to press forward and make up for lost ground.
"Right now, the harvest is lagging, but it is possible to harvest in Siberia until October, so we hope the situation will sort itself out," he said.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's spokesman, Viktor Konnov, said he thought the Siberian harvest could still help to offset poor crops in other parts of the country.
"In some regions, including Altai and Siberia, the harvest may be better than in the European regions," he said. "They may be able to provide for other parts of Russia.

Kaglashkin said new combines had been sent to Siberia on Kremlin orders. But he said the machines, which the government expected Siberian producers to equip with engines, would not significantly affect final output.
All hopes were pinned on better weather, Kaglashkin said, adding, "There are no other factors."
